analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $3.35 to $4.35 an hour over two years.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the two-year Congress expired.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to raise the federal minimum wage in steps: to $3.85 an hour in 1990 and $4.35 an hour starting in 1991, up from $3.35 [S2][S3]. That raise would apply to workers covered by the federal wage floor, many of them in retail, restaurants, and other low-paying jobs. The bill was introduced in February 1989, referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor, and sent to its Subcommittee on Labor Standards in April 1989 [S5]. No further action was taken before the 101st Congress ended in January 1991 [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage would gain a raise of up to $1.00 an hour, phased in over two years — roughly a 30% increase in the wage floor. Their households would see higher take-home pay, and some low-wage workers in states without higher state minimums would benefit most.

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets the federal minimum wage at $3.85 an hour in 1990 and $4.35 an hour from 1991 onward, up from $3.35 [S2][S3].
The increase is a direct raise in the wage floor for workers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act, the law that sets the national minimum wage [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay minimum-wage workers — especially small businesses and labor-intensive industries like restaurants and retail — would bear higher payroll costs, which could be passed to consumers through prices or absorbed through reduced hiring or hours.

drawbacks.text: Raising the minimum wage increases labor costs for employers of low-wage workers, a cost small businesses and labor-intensive industries argued would reduce hiring or raise prices.

The bill was a simple two-step increase with no phase-in flexibility, small-business exemptions, or regional cost-of-living adjustments, so it imposed the same wage floor nationwide regardless of local conditions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have delivered a substantial raise — about 30% over two years — to workers at the bottom of the pay scale, at a real but manageable cost to their employers. Its main design limitation is that it contained none of the compromises (longer phase-ins, training wages, exemptions) that later minimum-wage bills used to blunt employer objections, which may have made it easier to ignore in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to a House committee and then a subcommittee in the spring of 1989, and it never came out for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gerald Kleczka introduced the bill on February 23, 1989, to raise the minimum wage to $3.85 in 1990 and $4.35 thereafter [S1][S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor the same day [S5].
On April 5, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, where no further action followed [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors and died at the end of the 101st Congress on January 3, 1991, without a hearing result, a floor vote, or passage by either chamber [S1][S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers were better off, since no increase in the federal wage floor took effect from this bill. Workers earning the minimum wage gained nothing from it, though a different minimum-wage increase was enacted later in 1989 through separate legislation.

for.name: Rep. Gerald Kleczka
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the minimum wage to $4.35 an hour and referred it to committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other member cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape of support or opposition is unknown from the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: As a labor-intensive industry with many minimum-wage workers, it would have faced the largest payroll cost increases from the raise. Its costs would fall on consumers through prices or on workers through reduced hiring.
Retail employs large numbers of workers at or near the minimum wage, so a $1.00-an-hour increase would raise costs across the sector.
